papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: How Post-Training Reshapes LLMs: A Mechanistic View on Knowledge, Truthfulness, Refusal, and Confidence
papers.research_question: How does post-training affect the internal mechanisms of large language models in terms of knowledge storage, truthfulness, refusal, and confidence?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a mechanistic analysis of how post-training affects LLMs internally, revealing which mechanisms are preserved (e.g., knowledge storage locations, truthfulness direction) and which are altered (e.g., refusal direction), with implications for model steering and interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Post-training preserves some internal mechanisms (like knowledge storage and truthfulness direction) and alters others (like refusal direction), providing insights for model steering and future research in interpretability and LLM post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations in LLMs.
Post-training adapts knowledge representations from the base model while also developing new ones.
The truthfulness direction is highly similar between base and post-trained models and is effectively transferable for interventions.
The refusal direction differs between base and post-trained models and shows limited forward transferability.
Differences in confidence between base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons.
papers.limitation: Complex, multi-step processes such as reasoning and instruction-following are not well-captured by current mechanistic interpretability tools, limiting the scope of analysis.
future_direction: Design better post-training methods based on mechanistic insights.
Extend analysis to other capabilities like reasoning and instruction-following.
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for the success of large language models (LLMs), transforming pre-trained base models into more useful and aligned post-trained models. While plenty of works have studied post-training algorithms and evaluated post-training models by their outputs, it remains understudied how post-training reshapes LLMs internally. In this paper, we compare base and post-trained LLMs mechanistically from four perspectives to better understand post-training effects. Our findings across model families and datasets reveal that: (1) Post-training does not change the factual knowledge storage locations, and it adapts knowledge representations from the base model while developing new knowledge representations; (2) Both truthfulness and refusal can be represented by vectors in the hidden representation space. The truthfulness direction is highly similar between the base and post-trained model, and it is effectively transferable for interventions; (3) The refusal direction is different between the base and post-trained models, and it shows limited forward transferability; (4) Differences in confidence between the base and post-trained models cannot be attributed to entropy neurons. Our study provides insights into the fundamental mechanisms preserved and altered during post-training, facilitates downstream tasks like model steering, and could potentially benefit future research in interpretability and LLM post-training. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HZD01/post-training-mechanistic-analysis.

papers.title: Rectifying Belief Space via Unlearning to Harness LLMs' Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why do large language models generate incorrect answers, and can rectifying their belief space via unlearning spurious beliefs improve reasoning reliability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to rectify LLMs' belief space by identifying spurious beliefs via Forward-Backward Beam Search and unlearning them, improving reasoning accuracy and generalization on question answering tasks.
papers.conclusion: Rectifying the belief space via unlearning spurious beliefs effectively reduces erroneous reasoning in LLMs and improves generalization, offering a promising direction for enhancing reliability.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves accuracy on previously misanswered questions without degrading overall model performance.
It enhances generalization on unseen evaluation data.
Most beliefs identified are newly formed, not directly memorized from training data.
Forward-Backward Beam Search (FBBS) generates more effective beliefs than baseline generation methods.
Using the top-1 belief for unlearning is sufficient for performance gains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can exhibit advanced reasoning yet still generate incorrect answers. We hypothesize that such errors frequently stem from spurious beliefs, propositions the model internally considers true but are incorrect. To address this, we propose a method to rectify the belief space by suppressing these spurious beliefs while simultaneously enhancing true ones, thereby enabling more reliable inferences. Our approach first identifies the beliefs that lead to incorrect or correct answers by prompting the model to generate textual explanations, using our Forward-Backward Beam Search (FBBS). We then apply unlearning to suppress the identified spurious beliefs and enhance the true ones, effectively rectifying the model's belief space. Empirical results on multiple QA datasets and LLMs show that our method corrects previously misanswered questions without harming overall model performance. Furthermore, our approach yields improved generalization on unseen data, suggesting that rectifying a model's belief space is a promising direction for mitigating errors and enhancing overall reliability.

papers.title: The First Impression Problem: Internal Bias Triggers Overthinking in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Reasoning models often exhibit overthinking, characterized by redundant reasoning steps. We identify \emph{internal bias} elicited by the input question as a key trigger of such behavior. Upon encountering a problem, the model immediately forms a preliminary guess about the answer, which we term an internal bias since it may not be explicitly generated, and it arises without systematic reasoning. When this guess conflicts with its subsequent reasoning, the model tends to engage in excessive reflection, resulting in wasted computation. We validate the association between internal bias and overthinking across multiple models and diverse reasoning tasks. To demonstrate the causal relationship more rigorously, we conduct two counterfactual interventions, showing that removing the input question after the model reduces the redundant reasoning across various complex reasoning tasks, and manually injecting bias affects overthinking accordingly. Further interpretability experiments suggest that excessive attention to the input question serves as a key mechanism through which internal bias influences subsequent reasoning trajectories. Finally, we evaluated several methods aimed at mitigating overthinking, yet the influence of internal bias persisted under all conditions.

papers.title: KUDA: Knowledge Unlearning by Deviating Representation for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to effectively remove specific knowledge from large language models while retaining model utility?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes KUDA, a representation-level unlearning method that integrates unlearning layer selection, representation deviation, and relaxation null-space projection to remove target knowledge while effectively retaining LLM utility.
papers.conclusion: KUDA effectively removes target knowledge from LLMs while preserving model utility, offering a promising solution for safety and privacy concerns.
papers.key_findings:
KUDA outperforms existing baselines by effectively balancing knowledge removal and model utility retention.
KUDA achieves near-complete removal of target knowledge with marginal utility degradations (e.g., 3.1% on MUSE, 1.7% on WMDP).
KUDA maintains near-orthogonal gradient directions between forgetting and retention objectives, mitigating optimization conflicts.
A two-stage tuning strategy simplifies hyperparameter optimization into two decoupled linear searches.
KUDA demonstrates robust generalizability across modern models like Llama-3.1 and Qwen-3.
papers.limitation:
KUDA requires a retaining set Dr that shares a similar representation distribution with Df to achieve optimal performance.
The method assumes knowledge is stored in FFNs, which may not hold for all types of knowledge or models.
Causal tracing incurs substantial computational overhead.
future_direction: Extending KUDA to multimodal unlearning.
Exploring more efficient null-space projection techniques.
Investigating the theoretical guarantees of null-space projection.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) acquire a large amount of knowledge through pre-training on vast and diverse corpora. While this endows LLMs with strong capabilities in generation and reasoning, it amplifies risks associated with sensitive, copyrighted, or harmful content in training data.LLM unlearning, which aims to remove specific knowledge encoded within models, is a promising technique to reduce these risks. However, existing LLM unlearning methods often force LLMs to generate random or incoherent answers due to their inability to alter the encoded knowledge precisely. To achieve effective unlearning at the knowledge level of LLMs, we propose Knowledge Unlearning by Deviating representAtion (KUDA). We first utilize causal tracing to locate specific layers for target knowledge storage. We then design a new unlearning objective that induces the model's representations to deviate from its original position in the phase of knowledge removal, thus disrupting the ability to associate with the target knowledge. To resolve the optimization conflicts between forgetting and retention, we employ a relaxation null-space projection mechanism to mitigate the disruption to the representation space of retaining knowledge. Extensive experiments on representative benchmarks, WMDP and MUSE, demonstrate that KUDA outperforms most existing baselines by effectively balancing knowledge removal and model utility retention.

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does this paper investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their internal states through concept injection experiments.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited but functional introspective awareness, which is unreliable but may improve with model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models can detect and identify injected concepts in their activations.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed to think about concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not pin down specific mechanistic explanations.
Concept injection places models in an unnatural setting.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Investigating the grounding of emotional responses in introspective reports
Exploring introspective capabilities in more natural conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states. It is difficult to answer this question through conversation alone, as genuine introspection cannot be distinguished from confabulations. Here, we address this challenge by injecting representations of known concepts into a model's activations, and measuring the influence of these manipulations on the model's self-reported states. We find that models can, in certain scenarios, notice the presence of injected concepts and accurately identify them. Models demonstrate some ability to recall prior internal representations and distinguish them from raw text inputs. Strikingly, we find that some models can use their ability to recall prior intentions in order to distinguish their own outputs from artificial prefills. In all these experiments, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, the most capable models we tested, generally demonstrate the greatest introspective awareness; however, trends across models are complex and sensitive to post-training strategies. Finally, we explore whether models can explicitly control their internal representations, finding that models can modulate their activations when instructed or incentivized to "think about" a concept. Overall, our results indicate that current language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their own internal states. We stress that in today's models, this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent; however, it may continue to develop with further improvements to model capabilities.

papers.title: Does Localization Inform Unlearning? A Rigorous Examination of Local Parameter Attribution for Knowledge Unlearning in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does localization (identifying parameter regions responsible for knowledge) inform effective knowledge unlearning in language models? Specifically, is parameter locality indicative of effective knowledge removal?
papers.core_contribution: The paper challenges the assumption that localization informs unlearning, showing that unlearning can be achieved through multiple alternative parameter regions and that the set of parameters to be updated is not strictly determined.
papers.conclusion: Localization does not provide an effective basis for unlearning, challenging the core assumption that parameter locality is inherently indicative of effective knowledge removal.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning over randomly selected regions can outperform unlearning over regions selected by existing localization methods.
Even when unlearning is performed on the ground-truth region (oracle), it does not necessarily yield a better trade-off between forgetting and retention compared to random regions.
The set of parameters that must be modified for effective unlearning is not strictly determined.
The model may achieve ideal unlearning via flexible parameter adaptation rather than reverting to a specific parameter state.
papers.limitation:
Assumes MLPs are the primary components for knowledge storage and does not consider other components like attention layers.
Reformulation of MemFlex and WAGLE to score value vectors may not reflect the original design intentions.
Controlled experimental setup (updating only a target region) is not a realistic scenario, and generalization to full-parameter updates is unclear.
papers.abstract: Large language models often retain unintended content, prompting growing interest in knowledge unlearning. Recent approaches emphasize localized unlearning, restricting parameter updates to specific regions in an effort to remove target knowledge while preserving unrelated general knowledge. However, their effectiveness remains uncertain due to the lack of robust and thorough evaluation of the trade-off between the competing goals of unlearning. In this paper, we begin by revisiting existing localized unlearning approaches. We then conduct controlled experiments to rigorously evaluate whether local parameter updates causally contribute to unlearning. Our findings reveal that the set of parameters that must be modified for effective unlearning is not strictly determined, challenging the core assumption of localized unlearning that parameter locality is inherently indicative of effective knowledge removal.

papers.title: Do Llamas Work in English? On the Latent Language of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: Do multilingual language models trained on English-dominated corpora use English as an internal pivot language?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual transformers like Llama-2 use English as an internal pivot language, with intermediate layers representing concepts in English before mapping to the target language, indicating an English bias in their internal representations.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual LLMs have an English bias in their internal representations, which may lead to linguistic biases and has implications for equitable AI.
papers.key_findings:
In translation tasks, intermediate layers decode the English version of the correct next token before switching to the target language.
The forward pass goes through three phases: input space, concept space (biased towards English), and output space.
Token energy is low in middle layers, indicating that latents are in a concept space orthogonal to token space.
The English bias is less pronounced for languages with single-token words (like Chinese) in repetition tasks.
The same pattern is observed in Mistral-7B, suggesting generality of the phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Focus on Llama-2 family, so claims may not generalize to other models.
Tasks are simple and controlled, not real-world.
Limited understanding of the concept space structure.
Logit lens only reveals part of the internal state.
future_direction: Investigate how English bias affects downstream model behavior.
Study how English bias changes with different training data or tokenizers.
Extend to a wider range of tasks and models.

papers.title: The Vector Grounding Problem
papers.research_question: Can large language models (LLMs) have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded in the world, i.e., have intrinsic meaning, despite being trained only on text data without direct interaction with the world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve referential grounding (intrinsic meaning) through selection processes in training that endow internal states with representational functions, even without multimodality or embodiment.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can, in principle and in some cases in practice, have internal states and outputs that are referentially grounded, thus solving the Vector Grounding Problem and possessing intrinsic meaning independently of human interpretation.
papers.key_findings:
Distinguishes referential grounding from other forms (sensorimotor, relational, communicative, epistemic) and argues referential grounding is the only kind essential to solving the Vector Grounding Problem.
Proposes that referential grounding requires two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories: causal-informational relations to the world and a history of selection that endows internal states with the function of carrying this information.
Argues that post-training (e.g., preference tuning for factual accuracy) can establish selection processes that confer world-involving representational functions to LLM internal states.
Suggests that pre-training might, under specific conditions, also lead to world-involving representational functions through implicit extra-linguistic success conditions in the training data.
Contends that in-context learning could, in principle, allow LLMs to acquire world-involving representational functions during inference without parameter updates.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce seemingly meaningful outputs, yet they are trained on text alone without direct interaction with the world. This leads to a modern variant of the classical symbol grounding problem in AI: can LLMs' internal states and outputs be about extra-linguistic reality, independently of the meaning human interpreters project onto them? We argue that they can. We first distinguish referential grounding -- the connection between a representation and its worldly referent -- from other forms of grounding and argue it is the only kind essential to solving the problem. We contend that referential grounding is achieved when a system's internal states satisfy two conditions derived from teleosemantic theories of representation: (1) they stand in appropriate causal-informational relations to the world, and (2) they have a history of selection that has endowed them with the function of carrying this information. We argue that LLMs can meet both conditions, even without multimodality or embodiment.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: How large language models encode theory-of-mind: a study on sparse parameter patterns
papers.research_question: Which parameters in LLMs are sensitive to Theory-of-Mind capabilities, and how do these parameters influence ToM reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to identify extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameters in LLMs and shows that these parameters are linked to RoPE positional encoding, affecting attention mechanisms and degrading ToM performance when perturbed.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that ToM capabilities in LLMs are governed by sparse, low-rank parameter patterns linked to positional encoding and attention mechanisms, providing insights into how LLMs perform social reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
An extremely sparse ToM-sensitive parameter pattern exists, whose perturbation significantly affects RoPE-based models' ToM capabilities, while random perturbations do not. This degradation is linked to a reduction in contextual localization and language understanding.
The functionality of the ToM-sensitive parameter pattern relates to the positional encoding module in LLM architectures. Perturbing the pattern in LLMs with RoPE disrupts dominant frequency activations, impairing contextual localization. LLMs without RoPE lack this frequency-dependent activation structure and exhibit different sensitivity patterns.
Perturbing ToM-sensitive parameter patterns affects the attention mechanism, thereby influencing language understanding. It alters the angle between q and k_BOS under positional encoding, destabilizing the attention sink and distorting the attention matrix.
papers.limitation: The study focuses only on false-belief tasks (unexpected contents and transfer) and does not evaluate the full spectrum of ToM abilities.
future_direction: Leveraging ToM-sensitive parameters for targeted model alignment to ensure AI systems align with human ethical norms while mitigating unintended social biases.
Comparing the identified sparse parameter structures to neural representations of ToM in the human brain for comparative cognitive modeling.
Investigating if targeted attacks could degrade LLM reasoning abilities given that ToM capabilities depend on sparse and structured parameter subsets, for robustness and adversarial testing.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the emergence of Theory-of-Mind (ToM) capabilities in large language models (LLMs) from a mechanistic perspective, focusing on the role of extremely sparse parameter patterns. We introduce a novel method to identify ToM-sensitive parameters and reveal that perturbing as little as 0.001% of these parameters significantly degrades ToM performance while also impairing contextual localization and language understanding. To understand this effect, we analyze their interactions with core architectural components of LLMs. Our findings demonstrate that these sensitive parameters are closely linked to the positional encoding module, particularly in models using Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), where perturbations disrupt dominant frequency activations critical for contextual processing. Furthermore, we show that perturbing ToM-sensitive parameters affects LLMs’ attention mechanism by modulating the angle between queries and keys under positional encoding. These insights provide a deeper understanding of how LLMs acquire social reasoning abilities, bridging AI interpretability with cognitive science.

papers.title: Don't Make It Up: Preserving Ignorance Awareness in LLM Fine-Tuning
papers.research_question: How can we fine-tune LLMs to incorporate new knowledge without eroding their aligned epistemic abstention behavior (the ability to acknowledge when the model does not know)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SEAT, a fine-tuning method that combines sparse updates and entity-perturbed regularization to preserve a model's epistemic abstention (ability to say 'I don't know') while adapting it to new knowledge, without requiring alignment data or post-hoc re-alignment.
papers.conclusion: SEAT is an effective method for preserving epistemic abstention during knowledge adaptation, establishing preservation of abstention as a useful objective for safer model adaptation.
papers.key_findings:
SEAT preserves epistemic abstention on unseen queries (improving human-evaluated abstention by 18%–101% over baselines) while maintaining near-perfect target knowledge acquisition.
Both sparse training and entity-perturbed regularization are essential for SEAT's strong performance; ablations show each component alone is insufficient.
SEAT constrains activation drift on unseen data, keeping representations anchored near the base model's, while allowing meaningful shifts for fine-tuning data.
SEAT outperforms a range of baselines including full fine-tuning, LoRA, EWC, CLoRA, R-tuning, and experience replay in preserving abstention behavior.
SEAT preserves downstream utility across a diverse range of tasks (e.g., truthfulness, QA, reasoning) compared to the base model.
papers.limitation:
The optimal sparsity ratio needs to be tuned to balance learning efficacy and abstention preservation.
The method is empirically grounded and does not provide formal guarantees.
papers.abstract: Existing work on mitigating catastrophic forgetting during large language models (LLMs) fine-tuning for new knowledge instances has primarily focused on preserving performance on previously seen data, while critically overlooking the collapse of essential capabilities instilled through alignment, most notably the model's ability to faithfully express epistemic uncertainty (a property we term 'Ignorance Awareness'). In this work, we formalize the notion of Ignorance Awareness and illustrate that conventional fine-tuning methods can result in substantial activation displacement. This displacement undermines the critical capability of ignorance awareness, leading to undesirable behaviors such as hallucinations. To address this challenge, we introduce SEAT, a simple and principled fine-tuning approach that not only enables the model to effectively acquire new knowledge instances but also preserves its aligned ignorance awareness. SEAT integrates two key components: (1) sparse tuning that constrains activation drift, and (2) a novel entity perturbation method designed to counter knowledge entanglement. Experimental results demonstrate that, across both real-world and synthetic datasets, SEAT significantly outperforms baselines in preserving ignorance awareness while retaining optimal fine-tuning performance, offering a more robust solution for LLM fine-tuning.

papers.title: Answer When Needed, Forget When Not: Language Models Pretend to Forget via In-Context Knowledge Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can large language models be enabled to selectively forget specific information at test-time based on the query context?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method for in-context knowledge unlearning that enables LLMs to selectively forget information at test-time, and finds that LLMs 'pretend to forget' by making the decision only at the last layer while preserving correct predictions internally.
papers.conclusion: The in-context knowledge unlearning method enables LLMs to dynamically forget information at test-time and reveals that they 'pretend to forget', which is a significant step towards more ethically responsible and privacy-conscious AI.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves up to 95% forget accuracy while retaining 80% of unrelated knowledge, significantly outperforming baselines.
Internal behavior analysis using the logit lens reveals that fine-tuned LLMs generate correct predictions in middle layers and sustain them to the final layer, but the decision to output 'forgot' occurs only at the last layer.
LoRA tuning provides the most balanced performance across in-domain and out-of-domain scenarios compared to full fine-tuning and last-layer tuning.
The unlearning process does not significantly degrade the model's general language-understanding capabilities on standard NLP benchmarks.
The method enables test-time unlearning with non-hallucinated outputs (outputting 'forgot'), addressing limitations of prior approaches.
papers.limitation:
The method is difficult to apply to closed models accessible only via APIs (e.g., GPT-3, ChatGPT) because they do not allow architectural modifications or training procedure changes.
For closed models, internal behavior analysis during unlearning is not possible, hindering verification of the 'pretend to forget' behavior and optimization.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are applied across diverse domains, the ability to selectively unlearn specific information is becoming increasingly essential.For instance, LLMs are expected to selectively provide confidential information to authorized internal users, such as employees or trusted partners, while withholding it from external users, including the general public and unauthorized entities.Therefore, we propose a novel method termed "in-context knowledge unlearning", which enables the model to selectively forget information in test-time based on the query context.Our method fine-tunes pre-trained LLMs to enable prompt unlearning of target knowledge within the context, while preserving unrelated information.Experiments on TOFU, AGE and RWKU datasets using Llama2-7B/13B and Mistral-7B models demonstrate that our method achieves up to 95% forget accuracy while retaining 80% of unrelated knowledge, significantly outperforming baselines in both indomain and out-of-domain scenarios.Further investigation of the model's internal behavior revealed that while fine-tuned LLMs generate correct predictions in the middle layers and preserve them up to the final layer.However, the decision to forget is made only at the last layer, i.e. "LLMs pretend to forget".Our findings offer valuable insight into the improvement of the robustness of the unlearning mechanisms in LLMs, laying a foundation for future research in the field.

papers.title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the behavior of large language models indicate belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring as defined by the HOT-3 indicator for consciousness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework and the Belief Dominance metric to test the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs, providing empirical evidence for belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the existence of agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs, contributing to the study of AI consciousness.
papers.key_findings:
External manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation.
Belief formation causally drives the model's action selection.
Models can monitor and report their own belief states, indicating meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic implementation of belief formation, action selection, and meta-cognition remains unclear.
The framework is restricted to capturing beliefs that can be expressed in words.
The framework currently only tests two competing beliefs.
future_direction: Studying the mechanistic implementation of belief formation and meta-cognitive monitoring.
Extending the framework to capture latent beliefs beyond existing vocabulary.
Testing additional consciousness criteria in more capable models.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
papers.research_question: What is the internal computational structure of language models, and how do they respond to ablations? The paper investigates self-repair mechanisms (Hydra effect) and erasure functions in MLP layers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies two internal self-repair motifs in language models: the Hydra effect (downstream attention layers compensate for ablated layers) and erasure by late MLP layers (which downregulate the maximum-likelihood token).
papers.conclusion: The Hydra effect and erasure MLPs complicate circuit-level attribution and have implications for interpretability research, suggesting that assigning semantics to MLP neurons may be more difficult and that ablation studies must account for downstream compensatory changes.
papers.key_findings:
Language models exhibit the Hydra effect: ablating an attention layer causes a downstream attention layer to increase its impact to compensate.
Late MLP layers have an erasure function, acting to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token, and this effect is attenuated when attention layers are ablated.
Direct (unembedding-based) and total (ablation-based) importance measures are poorly correlated in most layers, except late layers.
The compensatory response is highly correlated with changes in direct effect at intermediate layers, explaining up to 92% of variance at layer 23.
These self-repair effects occur even in models trained without dropout, suggesting they are inherent to the architecture or training.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is performed at the layer level and does not investigate finer-grained components like individual attention heads or activation directions.
The compensatory effect does not fully restore the output, indicating that ablations still have a nonzero total effect.
future_direction: How much does the Hydra effect occur across the entire training distribution? Does sequence length play any role?
What are the Hydra effect attention heads responding to in the residual stream?
Do the same downstream heads act as Hydra effect replacement heads across multiple contexts?
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal structure of language model computations using causal analysis and demonstrate two motifs: (1) a form of adaptive computation where ablations of one attention layer of a language model cause another layer to compensate (which we term the Hydra effect) and (2) a counterbalancing function of late MLP layers that act to downregulate the maximum-likelihood token. Our ablation studies demonstrate that language model layers are typically relatively loosely coupled (ablations to one layer only affect a small number of downstream layers). Surprisingly, these effects occur even in language models trained without any form of dropout. We analyse these effects in the context of factual recall and consider their implications for circuit-level attribution in language models.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Semantic and Structural Analysis of Implicit Biases in Large Language Models: An Interpretable Approach
papers.research_question: How to identify and explain implicit stereotypes in large language models using an interpretable bias detection method?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable bias detection method for large language models that integrates nested semantic representation with attention perturbation to identify hidden social biases in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The interpretable detection method effectively identifies implicit biases in LLMs, improving detection accuracy and semantic consistency, and provides a foundation for bias intervention and ethical deployment.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method achieves higher bias detection accuracy (84.7%), semantic consistency (91.2%), and lower contextual sensitivity (8.5) compared to baselines.
It demonstrates strong generalization across multiple stereotype dimensions, with higher accuracy for gender and profession than for religion and race.
Higher semantic similarity between texts leads to more consistent bias judgments, reducing conflict rates.
Attention perturbation analysis reveals the model's sensitivity to social attribute terms, helping uncover bias pathways.
The method provides interpretable insights into how implicit stereotypes are formed in language models.
papers.limitation: Performance declines on more complex, culturally embedded biases such as religion and race due to their subtlety and ambiguity.
future_direction: Expand the method's adaptability to cross-cultural and multilingual contexts.
Integrate external knowledge bases and user feedback signals for more flexible bias detection.
Embed interpretability mechanisms into model interaction interfaces for user perception and response.
papers.abstract: This paper addresses the issue of implicit stereotypes that may arise during the generation process of large language models. It proposes an interpretable bias detection method aimed at identifying hidden social biases in model outputs, especially those semantic tendencies that are not easily captured through explicit linguistic features. The method combines nested semantic representation with a contextual contrast mechanism. It extracts latent bias features from the vector space structure of model outputs. Using attention weight perturbation, it analyzes the model's sensitivity to specific social attribute terms, thereby revealing the semantic pathways through which bias is formed. To validate the effectiveness of the method, this study uses the StereoSet dataset, which covers multiple stereotype dimensions including gender, profession, religion, and race. The evaluation focuses on several key metrics, such as bias detection accuracy, semantic consistency, and contextual sensitivity. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves strong detection performance across various dimensions. It can accurately identify bias differences between semantically similar texts while maintaining high semantic alignment and output stability. The method also demonstrates high interpretability in its structural design. It helps uncover the internal bias association mechanisms within language models. This provides a more transparent and reliable technical foundation for bias detection. The approach is suitable for real-world applications where high trustworthiness of generated content is required.

papers.title: DeCoT: Debiasing Chain-of-Thought for Knowledge-Intensive Tasks in Large Language Models via Causal Intervention
papers.research_question: How does internal knowledge bias in large language models impair chain-of-thought reasoning, and how can this bias be mitigated via causal intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal view to explain internal knowledge bias in LLMs and introduces DeCoT, a method that uses external knowledge as an instrumental variable and front-door adjustment to debias chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: DeCoT effectively alleviates the spurious correlation caused by internal knowledge bias, enabling LLMs to generate more accurate and logically sound chain-of-thought reasoning and final answers.
papers.key_findings:
Internal knowledge bias in LLMs can trigger the use of irrelevant information in prompts, leading to incoherent reasoning chains that impair logical reasoning.
DeCoT, by estimating the average causal effect (ACE) of CoT paths and sampling CoTs with high ACE, effectively reduces spurious correlation and improves reasoning accuracy.
The method consistently improves performance across multiple knowledge-intensive tasks and LLM backbones compared to standard CoT and context-aware contrastive decoding baselines.
DeCoT is compatible with and can improve other reasoning frameworks like ReAct by incorporating counterfactual debiasing.
The number of selected entities and alternative entities for causal intervention impacts performance, with more entities generally leading to better results but at increased computational cost.
papers.limitation: As an inference-stage causal intervention method, the improvement is limited by the upper bound of the LLM's capacity.
future_direction: Incorporate unbiased causal learning methods in the model pretraining or instruction tuning stage for more robust CoT reasoning.
Study the theoretical causal foundation of CoT prompting's mediator role in LLMs for better interpretability.
papers.abstract: Junda Wu, Tong Yu, Xiang Chen, Haoliang Wang, Ryan Rossi, Sungchul Kim, Anup Rao, Julian McAuley. Proceedings of the 62nd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2024.

papers.title: Birds have four legs?! NumerSense: Probing Numerical Commonsense Knowledge of Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Does and to what extent do pre-trained language models capture numerical commonsense knowledge, and how robust is this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a probing task and dataset (NumerSense) to evaluate numerical commonsense knowledge in pre-trained language models, finding that models perform poorly and are brittle to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Powerful pre-trained models such as BERT and RoBERTa perform surprisingly poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge even after fine-tuning, and the introduced dataset provides a basis for future improvement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT and RoBERTa perform poorly on numerical commonsense knowledge without fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning with distant supervision improves performance but still far from human performance.
Models are brittle to adversarial examples (e.g., inserting adjectives).
Attention analysis shows that important words for numerical commonsense (subject/object) receive low attention weights.
Open-domain QA models also perform poorly on 'how-many' questions derived from NumerSense.
future_direction: Improving PTLMs' abilities to faithfully capture (numerical) commonsense.
Populating numerical facts in current commonsense knowledge bases.
Improving open-domain QA for 'how-many' questions.
Incorporating more structured inductive biases (e.g., dependencies and semantic roles) in pre-training.
Controlling bias in masked language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent works show that pre-trained language models (PTLMs), such as BERT, possess certain commonsense and factual knowledge. They suggest that it is promising to use PTLMs as "neural knowledge bases" via predicting masked words. Surprisingly, we find that this may not work for numerical commonsense knowledge (e.g., a bird usually has two legs). In this paper, we investigate whether and to what extent we can induce numerical commonsense knowledge from PTLMs as well as the robustness of this process. To study this, we introduce a novel probing task with a diagnostic dataset, NumerSense, containing 13.6k masked-word-prediction probes (10.5k for fine-tuning and 3.1k for testing). Our analysis reveals that: (1) BERT and its stronger variant RoBERTa perform poorly on the diagnostic dataset prior to any fine-tuning; (2) fine-tuning with distant supervision brings some improvement; (3) the best supervised model still performs poorly as compared to human performance (54.06% vs 96.3% in accuracy).

papers.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the way knowledge is stored in MLP parameters and the performance of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Stronger large language models exhibit higher parameter specialization for knowledge storage in MLPs, and this specialization improves the efficiency of knowledge utilization and reduces hallucination.
papers.conclusion: Enhanced parameter specialization for knowledge storage correlates with superior performance in LLMs, and optimizing this specialization improves task performance and reduces hallucination, highlighting the importance of aligning knowledge storage with retrieval mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models show higher parameter specialization, with PSS correlating strongly with performance on knowledge tasks.
Parameter specialization increases with model scale within the same family.
Parameter specialization evolves during pretraining, increasing in later training steps.
Fine-tuning that enhances parameter specialization (FT-PV) improves performance on knowledge tasks and reduces hallucination compared to other fine-tuning strategies.
Specialized knowledge distribution helps compress knowledge and reduce interference from irrelevant information.
papers.limitation:
Only examined knowledge parameter specialization within the MLP, not attention modules.
Tested models only up to 14B parameters due to GPU limitations.
future_direction: Progressively narrow the focus to individual neurons to measure more precise Parameter Specialization.
Extend the concept to other model architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs).
papers.abstract: Over time, a growing wave of large language models from various series has been introduced to the community. Researchers are striving to maximize the performance of language models with constrained parameter sizes. However, from a microscopic perspective, there has been limited research on how to better store knowledge in model parameters, particularly within MLPs, to enable more effective utilization of this knowledge by the model. In this work, we analyze twenty publicly available open-source large language models to investigate the relationship between their strong performance and the way knowledge is stored in their corresponding MLP parameters. Our findings reveal that as language models become more advanced and demonstrate stronger knowledge capabilities, their parameters exhibit increased specialization. Specifically, parameters in the MLPs tend to be more focused on encoding similar types of knowledge. We experimentally validate that this specialized distribution of knowledge contributes to improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in these models. Furthermore, by conducting causal training experiments, we confirm that this specialized knowledge distribution plays a critical role in improving the model's efficiency in leveraging stored knowledge.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Discovering Bias in Latent Space: An Unsupervised Debiasing Approach
papers.research_question: Can we mitigate bias directly in the model representation space and do so without labeled data?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes STEER FAIR, an unsupervised inference-time activation steering algorithm that identifies bias directions in a model's representation space and steers activations away from them to mitigate bias, particularly option ordering bias in question-answering.
papers.conclusion: Introduces STEER FAIR, an approach for unsupervised mitigation of bias in question-answering models operating directly in the model representation space, which improves performance across benchmark tasks and matches supervised baselines.
papers.key_findings:
STEER FAIR significantly reduces instruction-tuned model performance variance across prompt modifications on three benchmark tasks.
The unsupervised method surpasses a supervised baseline (ITI) with 100 labels and matches performance with 500 labels.
The identified bias direction is generalizable across datasets with the same task.
Only a small number of unlabeled sample demonstrations are sufficient to identify effective bias directions.
Steering bias directions does not negatively impact base model performance.
papers.limitation:
The accurate identification of bias directions depends on the existence of directions in activation space that effectively summarize bias, requiring separation between usable knowledge and bias. The precise circumstances under which these conditions hold remain unclear.
Absence of theoretical characterizations for hyperparameters and the required number of unlabeled samples.
future_direction: Extension of the method to accommodate non-enumerable bias, such as exploring latent directions associated with harmful text generation or misinformation.
papers.abstract: The question-answering (QA) capabilities of foundation models are highly sensitive to prompt variations, rendering their performance susceptible to superficial, non-meaning-altering changes. This vulnerability often stems from the model's preference or bias towards specific input characteristics, such as option position or superficial image features in multi-modal settings. We propose to rectify this bias directly in the model's internal representation. Our approach, SteerFair, finds the bias direction in the model's representation space and steers activation values away from it during inference. Specifically, we exploit the observation that bias often adheres to simple association rules, such as the spurious association between the first option and correctness likelihood. Next, we construct demonstrations of these rules from unlabeled samples and use them to identify the bias directions. We empirically show that SteerFair significantly reduces instruction-tuned model performance variance across prompt modifications on three benchmark tasks. Remarkably, our approach surpasses a supervised baseline with 100 labels by an average of 10.86% accuracy points and 12.95 score points and matches the performance with 500 labels.

papers.title: StressPrompt: Does Stress Impact Large Language Models and Human Performance Similarly?
papers.research_question: Does stress impact Large Language Models and human performance similarly? This study explores whether LLMs exhibit stress responses similar to humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the StressPrompt dataset and stress scanner to evaluate LLMs under stress, finding that LLMs exhibit human-like stress-performance patterns, with optimal performance under moderate stress.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit performance patterns similar to humans under stress, with moderate stress enhancing capabilities like reasoning and instruction following, while excessive stress impairs tasks like bias detection, suggesting that LLMs have captured human-like stress-performance dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform optimally under moderate stress and decline under low and high stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law.
Stress prompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, changing neural representations as measured by PCA on hidden states.
Different LLMs show varying sensitivity to stress, with architecture and training influencing responses.
Task complexity affects optimal stress levels, with complex tasks performing better at lower stress.
Stress impacts emotional intelligence and bias detection differently, improving emotional intelligence under moderate stress but worsening bias detection under high stress.
papers.abstract: Human beings often experience stress, which can significantly influence their performance. This study explores whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit stress responses similar to those of humans and whether their performance fluctuates under different stress-inducing prompts. To investigate this, we developed a novel set of prompts, termed StressPrompt, designed to induce varying levels of stress. These prompts were derived from established psychological frameworks and carefully calibrated based on ratings from human participants. We then applied these prompts to several LLMs to assess their responses across a range of tasks, including instruction-following, complex reasoning, and emotional intelligence. The findings suggest that LLMs, like humans, perform optimally under moderate stress, consistent with the Yerkes-Dodson law. Notably, their performance declines under both low and high-stress conditions. Our analysis further revealed that these StressPrompts significantly alter the internal states of LLMs, leading to changes in their neural representations that mirror human responses to stress. This research provides critical insights into the operational robustness and flexibility of LLMs, demonstrating the importance of designing AI systems capable of maintaining high performance in real-world scenarios where stress is prevalent, such as in customer service, healthcare, and emergency response contexts. Moreover, this study contributes to the broader AI research community by offering a new perspective on how LLMs handle different scenarios and their similarities to human cognition.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: HalluShift: Measuring Distribution Shifts towards Hallucination Detection in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in LLM-generated responses be detected by analyzing distribution shifts in internal states and token probabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HalluShift, a hallucination detection method that analyzes distribution shifts in internal states and token probabilities, eliminating the need for manual layer selection and external knowledge.
papers.conclusion: HalluShift effectively detects hallucinations by analyzing internal dynamics, providing a robust and efficient solution for hallucination detection in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
HalluShift outperforms existing methods on multiple benchmarks, achieving significant improvements in AUC-ROC.
The method generalizes well across different datasets and models.
Distribution shift features, particularly Wasserstein distance, are the most important for detection.
A window size of 2 for layer-wise analysis yields the best performance.
The method is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass.
future_direction: Explicit regularization during LLM training with an auxiliary objective
Activation-shifting towards a truthful direction during inference
Integration of HalluShift into reinforcement learning-based fine-tuning for automated feedback
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently garnered widespread attention due to their adeptness at generating innovative responses to the given prompts across a multitude of domains. However, LLMs often suffer from the inherent limitation of hallucinations and generate incorrect information while maintaining well-structured and coherent responses. In this work, we hypothesize that hallucinations stem from the internal dynamics of LLMs. Our observations indicate that, during passage generation, LLMs tend to deviate from factual accuracy in subtle parts of responses, eventually shifting toward misinformation. This phenomenon bears a resemblance to human cognition, where individuals may hallucinate while maintaining logical coherence, embedding uncertainty within minor segments of their speech. To investigate this further, we introduce an innovative approach, HalluShift, designed to analyze the distribution shifts in the internal state space and token probabilities of the LLM-generated responses. Our method attains superior performance compared to existing baselines across various benchmark datasets. Our codebase is available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/hallushift.

papers.title: CBEval: A framework for evaluating and interpreting cognitive biases in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive biases manifest in large language models, and can they be interpreted using a framework based on Shapley value analysis?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a framework (CBE VAL) using Shapley value analysis to interpret and understand a host of cognitive biases in frontier LLMs, introducing round number bias and the concept of a cognitive bias barrier.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully interprets cognitive shortcomings in LLMs, revealing biases that arise from training heuristics, model characteristics like in-context learning, and the training data itself, similar to human cognitive biases.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit several cognitive biases including framing effect, anchoring effect, representativeness heuristic, priming effect, and a newly identified round number bias.
Shapley value analysis can be used to construct influence graphs that identify the words and phrases most responsible for the manifested biases.
A cognitive bias barrier is identified, representing the point at which an LLM understands a lower loss percentage corresponds to a higher profit percentage.
Models like GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini show differences in their cognitive bias barriers, indicating varying levels of robustness in decision-making.
Anchoring and priming effects, while similar, are hypothesized to rely on different model mechanisms: anchoring on the attention mechanism and priming on associative mappings in MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on output probability distributions; model responses can change due to token noise rather than actual reasoning.
Different system prompts produce slightly different probability distributions, though the main findings hold.
